lead: Knuckle and cotter joints connect two rods that pull apart. A knuckle joint passes a pin through an eye and a fork, so it allows a little angular movement; a cotter joint drives a tapered flat cotter through a socket and a spigot, so it holds the rods rigidly in line. Each part fails in its own way, by tension, shear, crushing or bending, so the design is a chain of simple checks, one per failure mode. They are used in tie rods, valve rods, roof trusses, crane links and the piston rod to crosshead of steam engines.
prereq: You need direct tension, shear, crushing (bearing) and bending stress from the chapters on simple stresses.

sections.h3: Knuckle joint: parts and load path

blocks.text: One rod ends in an eye; the other ends in a fork with two tines. The eye sits between the tines and a pin passes through all three; a collar and a taper pin keep it in place. The pull P goes from the eye into the middle of the pin and out through the two tines, so the pin has two shear planes: double shear.

Common starting proportions for rod diameter d are: pin diameter d₁ = d, outer diameter of eye d₂ = 2d, collar diameter 1.5d, eye thickness b = 1.25d and each fork tine a = 0.75d. Proportions only propose sizes; the stress checks decide them.

items: Pin in bending: M = (P/2)(b/4 + a/3) and σ<sub>b</sub> = 32M/(πd₁³). This assumes the eye load spread evenly over b and the tine loads varying over a. The simpler point-load model M = P(a + b)/4 is more cautious.
Eye in tension and in double shear across the hole: σ<sub>t</sub> = τ = P/[b(d₂ − d₁)].
Eye crushing on the pin: σ<sub>c</sub> = P/(b·d₁).
Fork in tension and shear: P/[2a(d₂ − d₁)]; fork crushing: P/(2a·d₁).

blocks.text: The pin is long compared with its diameter, so bending often decides it, not shear. A pin that passes the shear check can still bend.

sections.h3: Cotter joint: socket, spigot and cotter

blocks.text: In the socket-and-spigot cotter joint, one rod ends in a socket (a hollow end) and the other in a spigot with a collar. A flat cotter, tapered about 1 in 30 so it wedges tight and can be knocked out, passes through slots in both. With rod diameter d, spigot diameter d₂, socket outer diameter d₁, cotter thickness t and width b:

items: Spigot tension across the slot: P = [(π/4)d₂² − d₂t]σ<sub>t</sub>, usually with t = 0.31d₂.
Socket tension across the slot: P = [(π/4)(d₁² − d₂²) − (d₁ − d₂)t]σ<sub>t</sub>.
Spigot crushing on the cotter: P = d₂tσ<sub>c</sub>.
Socket collar crushing: P = (d₄ − d₂)tσ<sub>c</sub>, with d₄ its outer diameter.
Spigot collar crushing on the socket: P = (π/4)(d₃² − d₂²)σ<sub>c</sub>.

blocks.text: Ends beyond the slot also shear out: the spigot end needs a length a with P = 2a·d₂·τ.

examples.question: Design a knuckle joint for a tie rod pull of 50 kN. Permissible stresses: tension and bending 80 MPa, shear 50 MPa, crushing 90 MPa. Use the standard proportions, then check every part.
steps: Proportions: d₁ = 30 mm, d₂ = 60 mm, b = 1.25 × 30 = 37.5 mm, a = 0.75 × 30 = 22.5 mm.
Pin needed for bending: d₁ = (32 × 421 900/(π × 80))<sup>1/3</sup> = 37.7 mm; take d₁ = 38 mm (σ<sub>b</sub> = 78.3 MPa).
Eye with d₂ = 60 mm: P/[b(d₂ − d₁)] = 50 000/(37.5 × 22) = 60.6 MPa, above τ = 50. Raise d₂ to 66 mm: 50 000/(37.5 × 28) = 47.6 MPa, below both 50 and 80.
Eye crushing: 50 000/(37.5 × 38) = 35.1 MPa. Fork: tension and shear 50 000/(2 × 22.5 × 28) = 39.7 MPa; crushing 50 000/(2 × 22.5 × 38) = 29.2 MPa. All pass.
examples.answer: Rod 30 mm, pin 38 mm (set by bending, not shear), eye outer diameter 66 mm, eye 37.5 mm thick, tines 22.5 mm thick.

examples.question: A socket-and-spigot cotter joint carries 50 kN. Permissible stresses: tension 75 MPa, shear 60 MPa, crushing 100 MPa. Find d, d₂, t, d₁ and b.
steps: Spigot with t = 0.31d₂: 50 000 = (0.785 − 0.31)d₂² × 75 gives d₂ = 37.4 mm; take d₂ = 40 mm, t = 12.4 mm.
Spigot crushing with t = 12: 50 000/(40 × 12) = 104 MPa > 100. Take t = 13 mm: 96.2 MPa. Spigot tension: 50 000/(1256.6 − 520) = 67.9 MPa.
Socket: [(π/4)(d₁² − 1600) − 13(d₁ − 40)] × 75 = 50 000 gives d₁ = 51.3 mm; take 52 mm.
Cotter shear: b = 50 000/(2 × 13 × 60) = 32.1 mm; take b = 34 mm (τ = 56.6 MPa).
Spigot collar: d₃ = √(4 × 50 000/(π × 100) + 40²) = 47.3 mm, say 48 mm. Socket collar: d₄ = 40 + 50 000/(13 × 100) = 78.5 mm, say 80 mm.
examples.answer: d = 30 mm, d₂ = 40 mm, t = 13 mm, d₁ = 52 mm, b = 34 mm, d₃ = 48 mm, d₄ = 80 mm.

traps: Single shear for the knuckle pin. It has two shear planes: τ = 2P/(πd₁²).
Stopping after the shear check. In the worked example the 30 mm pin passes shear at 35 MPa but bends at 159 MPa.
Forgetting that the eye's net section is b(d₂ − d₁), not b·d₂.
Taking the cotter shear area as b × t once. The cotter has two shear planes: P = 2btτ.
Using the rod diameter for spigot crushing. Crushing is on d₂ × t, the projected contact of the cotter on the spigot.

quiz.q: Name the parts of a knuckle joint and of a cotter joint.
quiz.a: Knuckle: eye, fork, pin, collar and taper pin. Cotter joint: socket, spigot with collar, and cotter.

quiz.q: Why is a cotter given a taper, and why on one side only?
quiz.a: The taper (about 1 in 30) lets the cotter be driven in to pull the joint tight and knocked out to dismantle it. One taper is enough to wedge it; a small taper keeps it self-locking so it does not work loose.

quiz.q: A cotter 20 mm wide and 8 mm thick carries 30 kN. Find its shear stress.
A knuckle pin of 25 mm carries 60 kN. Find the shear stress.
If the knuckle pin diameter is doubled at the same load, how do its shear and bending stresses change?
quiz.a: Shear stress ∝ 1/d₁², so it becomes one quarter. Bending stress ∝ 1/d₁³, so it becomes one eighth (the moment arm b/4 + a/3 is unchanged if a and b stay the same).

quiz.q: Why is a knuckle joint used where the rods must swing, and a cotter joint where they must stay in line?
quiz.a: The knuckle pin acts as a hinge, so the rods can turn about it in one plane. The cotter wedges the spigot hard into the socket, so the rods cannot turn and the joint can also take compression.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern knuckle and clevis joints are bought as standard clevis pins and rod ends sized from catalogues. Their life is often set by fretting and wear at the pin, so bushes and grease nipples matter more than the static checks. Search for clevis pin standards and fretting fatigue of pinned joints.
